The House resumed, from Thursday, April 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-22, intituled Canadian Football Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, in the last seven or eight weeks the uproar over Bill C-22, the football bill, has both been positive and negative. Certainly, the members of the Toronto sports media would have people believe that a terrible thing is happening and is being permitted by the government of Canada. Certainly, members of the opposition party would like us to believe that as well, and the Canadian public to believe it. I noted, when the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) led off for the official opposition last night, that at no time during his amusing and sometimes interesting comments did he put weight on either of his feet when coming down on both sides of the fence. The hon. member for Hillsborough stressed that he spoke for the opposition, and that there are important and critical matters to be dealt with by the government and the House. That is quite true. The Liberal party recognizes that, as does the government, and I will be the final speaker on the government side. Yet this bill must progress, not only in fairness to the Canadian Football League, but also in fairness to the Northmen and John Bassett. It must be dealt with, surely, before the football season approaches. If this is not done real harm could be caused to fans in Toronto as well as to the Canadian Football League.
I remind my hon. friends opposite that the government was forced to legislate, after having made its policy eminently clear through the former minister of national health and welfare some 17 months ago, and reaffirmed by the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) when he took over that portfolio. The government was forced into legislating, and now this bill is before the House.
You know, filibuster can be a very effective technique for the opposition in times of majority government. It can be used to keep the majority from legislating something that the opposition feels is not in the public interest. However, the majority rests with the opposition parties at this time. There is no reason to prolong this debate. If members want to act responsibly, surely they will deal with the bill in fairness to the CFL and the Northmen before the football season begins. I hope there will be co-operation by all parties in the House so that we can get on with this matter. Many members on my side would like to participate. I think the hon. members for Sarnia-Lamb-ton (Mr. Cullen), Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), Spadina (Mr. Stollery), Labelle (Mr. Dupras) and others want to participate. They are satisfied, I believe, however, to work in committee, and have us get on with second reading.
The hon. member for Hillsborough said that the government and the House have more important things to do.
Canadian Professional Football
Hear, hear!

He said we are taking up important time. Well, I am pleased to see that I have the rapt attention of hon. members opposite because, so far, this debate has taken less than two hours of the time of the House. The bill could be dealt with in five or six hours, if the opposition wants to be co-operative. We want debate to be short. As I said, I am the final speaker.
You hope.

Well, we have not spent two hours so far debating this bill. All of us on both sides, especially those representing constituencies in Metropolitan Toronto, have received a great deal of mail. Answering it is very time consuming. Many of these letters say, why is the government spending so much time on this subject? I write back and say that the government is not; we have said what we want to do, and we want to get on with it. It takes me and my colleagues a great deal of time to reply to these letters. I note, having checked my files, that I have not received letters from these people covering such other matters as labour strife, inflation, justice, pensions and what have you, subjects which the opposition says must be dealt with. I agree. But sports are extremely important to Canadians, as you will agree if you look at the pages of coverage given sports in our newspapers and the attention our broadcasting media gives to the subject. It is of great interest to Canadians and that is why this bill is before us today.
The hon. member for Hillsborough made several other points to which I should like to reply. At one point he mentioned the domination of our colleges by foreign professors. That is the kind of red herring that party brings forward when it has no united policy of its own. It is clearly a matter of provincial jurisdiction. I wish the hon. member could talk to the government of Ontario, in which my constituency is, so that he could convince the government of Ontario to act on policies which my party has put forward provincially for several years to correct that situation. The hon. member for Hillsborough said, as the official lead-off speaker for his party, that it was "beyond his comprehension" that we were dealing with this subject at this time. He said that we should debate other matters. I say, let's finish this one, and have done. The strength of the majority is not on the government side; it is with the opposition parties. It will be "beyond the comprehension" of other parties in this House and the Canadian public if the opposition says that debate on the subject is beyond its comprehension but then delays.
The hon. member for Hillsborough's speech was perhaps the most entertaining I have heard since coming to the House. It was 40 minutes of witticisms, rhetoric and, at times, buffoonery. But I have found that when the Progressive Conservative Party have trouble facing an issue together, when they are seriously split, as they usually are, up goes this smokescreen. The Canadian public is well aware of their talent to cover division in their party and, so, their credibility goes up in smoke as well.
Just after I had been recognized to speak last evening, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) made the comment, "Let him dig his own grave." I am confident

Toronto has always been prepared to shed parochial, selfish advantage, if it is in the national interest to do so. The hon. member for York-Simcoe seriously underestimates the electorate of the greater Toronto area if he thinks that anyone will be elected or defeated because we did not follow our own self interest but rather what is good for Canada.
Before touching on the essentials of this legislation, I wish to make one final point of rebuttal to the comments made last evening by the hon. member for Hillsborough. He said that, lacking expertise, he was quoting Russ Jackson, who, he said, doubts the efficacy of the measure before the House. The Canadian Football League teams, the western cities directly affected, the Canadian Amateur Football Association and the players' association do not doubt the efficacy of this particular measure. They are all on record as supporting it strongly. They are not one football player but the entire football industry.
Ninety five per cent of the Toronto sports press has been strident in opposition to this move by the government. I suggest that there are some honest conflicts of interest, in that they want the benefit of this football club to Toronto. It might provide very good football, indeed. They also have some real conflicts of interest in who would be travelling with that team around the United States to cover its games and which of them now who are so stridently against the government are receiving moneys from the World Hockey League for play by play and colour comments on television and radio in Toronto?
Despite the organized lobby that I believe has been developing in support of the Northmen, including a letter writing campaign, in two months in a constituency of 160,000 people, I have received less than 40 letters. About one quarter of those letters are in support and they were not prompted by a strident campaign of the Northmen managers.
It has been suggested on several occasions that polls in Toronto suggest overwhelming support for the Northmen coming into Canada. I suggest that if we wrote polls with questions worded in the same way, we would be saying "Are you in favour of free ice cream?" If those polls had said "Are you in favour of it if the CFL is jeopardized", I suggest they would be very different. If they had said is Canadian football important, they would have been very different. If they would have asked whether the CFL and the Grey Cup game plays an important role in developing Canadianism, those polls would have been very different. The Northmen suggested along the way that the government has not offered a compromise and has not been willing to sit down. I suggest you cannot compromise on a situation where once they are here, and I will carry that argument further in a few minutes, the CFL team is lost.
Let me take up a couple of the arguments they have put forward as areas where they would compromise. One is on equalized payments. They say they would pay the largest amount they have ever paid, the amount that the Argonauts paid last year of equalization of $48,000. There is no mention of pre-season equalization which manages to

be a cost of $25,000 to $30,000. There is no mention of play-off equalization of $40,000 to $60,000. There is no mention of $150,000, but in fact $48,000, a very limited amount which would make very little difference to the survival of the CFL. They argue they would be the only franchise and they, the Northmen, control the rights in Canada. They say it would only be in Toronto. I think one team in Canada in the World Football League is as dangerous as two or three teams simply because of the great pride of Canadians and their great sense of competition.
You suddenly have the one Canadian David taking on the American Goliath. The three quarters of Canadians who can see American television will turn toward that because of their very pride and sense of Canadianism, but in time where will we be? If the one team is allowed, then where do we find the top of the pyramid where now our young people can develop in football, become the best, become professional and find nine teams in which to place themselves? Perhaps in an expanded CFL with London and perhaps Dartmouth-Halifax there would be an even larger top of the pyramid, but where when there is only one team? When they are looking for American super heroes, will those American teams, which can draw from 10 times the population, really start looking at Canadian talent? I doubt it very much.
If Toronto were allowed that WFL franchise, how could a government whose responsibility is the national interest possibly give a special deal to one Canadian city? Would we not then have to go ahead and allow what I believe will come about if this bill is not passed, namely an application from the National Football League for entry into Canada as well? Then, what will we have because with those two teams, there can be no doubt but that the CFL will die.
We will have two little brother football clubs in Canada playing all the big brothers in the United States. Then, where is Canadian football? Where is the incentive to develop Canadian football? Where is the east-west rivalry in Canadian football? Where are the five publicly owned western clubs? Where is the huge Canadian audience watching Canadian Grey Cup over Canadian television each year?
There are also the apples and bananas arguments that have been put forward. What about the Montreal Expos? The Montreal Expos came here and got assistance from the government in some tax forgiveness clauses simply because there was no major league baseball in Canada and because the government thought it would be good. For our largest city, Montreal, it is good. It attracts many fans, it is popular, provides entertainment and this government has no argument with it. On that same point, may I say that the same incentive and help is available for the development of a major league baseball club in Toronto. One of the people bound up in that and probably the person who will succeed in developing it is John Bassett Jr..
What about the NHL? Surely, that battle was lost some decades ago, not because of the most recent expansion, but away back when Canadian hockey began to involve itself with American cities. However, I cannot believe that yesterday's mistakes justify inaction today. We can protect a Canadian institution and, as a parliament, we should do that.

In Toronto there is concern about making the expanded stadium pay its own way if there is not a second football team. Well, I understand that the additional revenues from a second major league football club in Toronto would be about $200,000 a year. Much more than that would be provided if major league baseball came into that stadium simply because many more games would be played in that sport in that stadium each season. Three out of four American cities which tried two major football leagues failed, Dallas, Chicago and Los Angeles. The only one that succeeded was New York City which could draw on a population of almost 14 million.
What good relying on revenues from a second major league football club to support that stadium if within a year or two, as experience has shown, one of those teams would fail? If that happened, I suggest the team would be the Argonauts and goodbye Canadian Football League. I do not deny that the Northmen would bring new and exciting sports to Toronto but do we need it so much in Toronto? Is it so essential to us in addition to what we now have? Are we so short of good competitive sports and entertainment that we will ignore our western Canadian cities and fellow Canadian football fans?

There it is, Mr. Speaker. They all line up with the government.
Hear, hear!

I think it should be made clear that Bill C-22 is not an act against one single Canadian enterprise. It is for Canadian enterprise and for Canadian sports development. The CFL expansion has been brought about as part of the action of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. London can now have a franchise. Halifax-Dartmouth is open for expansion so it is truly national from coast to coast. I do agree with the comments in that part of the speech of the hon. member for Hillsborough last evening.
Over seven years, the training of young Canadians will be doubled to 500,000 or 600,000 in football. For Torontonians, the blackout will be lifted on an experimental basis
Canadian Professional Football when the expanded stadium is sold out. Exhibition games are encouraged. We can have the David and Goliath battle with the Americans. We can fill our great sense of competition and pride in competition with the American leagues but meanwhile protecting our own Canadian Football League.
The legislation is not negative. It is positive and it is for Canadians. The government of Canada has been making efforts to protect Canadian industry as long as this country has existed. Most recently the government acted against the DISC program in the United States with a measure that allowed corporate tax cuts. We have had tariffs, special grants to business, loans and all sorts of other incentives to help Canadian business in competition with foreign interests.
In the development of artistic talent, literature and sports, CRTC regulations have encouraged more Canadian development. John Bassett Sr. and John Bassett Jr., through Glen Warren Productions in Toronto as well as through CFTO, have developed with their own business expertise, which is recognized and respected, and with the rules set down by the CRTC one of the most successful television production and television operations in North America because the Canadian government provided special incentives and Canadian content rules. The Canadian Film Development Corporation has spent millions of dollars to develop the Canadian film industry because we in this country are in such tough competition with the United States. Hundreds of thousands of those millions have gone to Agincourt Productions and John Bassett Jr. for films like "Face Off", "Flick" and "Paperback Hero". It was his excellent entrepreneurship and this government's assistance that made it happen.
In 1972, John Bassett Sr. sought government financial assistance for the publicly owned western clubs in the CFL. Yet today many members opposite would like to argue, as the press reports, that though the government may wish to act against the Northmen it has no right to intrude in Canadian football. How does that gibe?
I see no financial hardship for the Northmen owners, Mr. Speaker. They will prosper if they run their team in the United States. I would not be unhappy to see a Canadian enterprise move into the United States for a change and if they sell it to an American city they also will profit. Meanwhile, the people involved in this operation can go on and develop baseball in Toronto on a major league level. They can go on with their Canadian films with government assistance, they can go on with their Canadian T.V. supported by government control of Canadian television. If the Northmen are allowed, the NFL in Montreal cannot be denied. That is the next step.
Is there a real possibility such a development would kill the CFL, Mr. Speaker? Well, the CFL teams think so, the Players Association thinks so, the Canadian Amateur Football Association thinks so, the Prairie Cities think so. All those important groups say that the CFL will be jeopardized, and if parliament respects those fears and believes Canadian football is of real importance to Canadians as a part of our lifestyle, then parliament will support this bill.

As I said when I began, Mr. Speaker, we want to have brief but meaningful debate. The government and the backbenches, certainly on this side, are not suggesting closure or the muffling of contrary views. We are prepared to complete our participation at this point, however, in the hope that this House can soon move on to other matters.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, let me begin by drawing the attention of the House of Commons and the country once again to the wide range of problems which beset us in Canada today. Inflation is running at a rate of approximately 10 per cent, the government is obviously disorganized-
Order!

-but instead of coming to grips with the situation which exists in the country we are here today discussing football. Earlier today, during question period, the point was made that, with all its articulated concern, with all its phoney interest in the country, the government has not brought down a single piece of legislation to deal with the economic and other ills which so badly affect us. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) excused himself by saying parliament had come to the aid of fishermen, farmers and small businessmen by passing legislation last week. I would point out that the only reason this bill was passed was that the party to which I belong preferred to stay here this week and work, and not run away to Barbados-
A cheap argument.

I want to deal with some of the remarks which were made by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Fleming) when, echoing his master's voice, he said his party had no interest in a filibuster and no interest in closure. The hon. member put forward on behalf of the government he supports a proposition which strains the credulity even of those who are accustomed to watching the way the government works. The government has placed before the House a bill which is clear evidence of its distorted priorities at a time of national emergency. It is the government which controls the business which is to be brought before the House, but having brought this bill forward, what does it do? It asks us not to talk about it. It tries to curtail the right of individual members to deal with the bill.
What's stopping you. Deal with it.

If the government is concerned about inflation, as the hon. member suggested it is, let them change their priorities and bring in legislation dealing with inflation. Let them not seek to mislead the House of Commons.
You are running scared!

That kind of approach indicates a double contempt for parliament; first, contempt by introducing legislation which ignores the obvious priorities, and, second, contempt by seeking, with all the means at its disposal-
Are you for or against Canadian football? That is the issue.
Let me suggest to you, Mr. Speaker-
Are you against a Canadian identity? Yes, or no?
I find it strange that a question about the Canadian identity should come from a minister who has responsibilities in this field but no staff at all, which indicates the kind of identity-
Come and see us some time.

One other matter before I come to the substance of the bill. I wish to refer to the suggestion by the minister yesterday, supported by that very great ability of his to count noses, that the bill did not involve a question of confidence. I want to ask the minister what right he had to state, in his place, out of the shadow of the grey eminence he used to occupy, that this is, or is not, a matter of confidence. Such a question is surely one for the House itself to consider.

speechtext: Read Beauchesne!

He makes such statements simply because he is having trouble getting the member who sits in front of him to support his legislation. The minister made the suggestion on television, which has now become the principal method used by ministers when they wish to make announcements, that this bill was a trade-off designed to help western Canada in exchange for concessions western Canada made in connection with the petroleum question. I shall not deal with this aspect at length, but I would make the point, as an Albertan, that if there is to be some kind of balance in confederation we in western Canada would much prefer that attention be given to our legitimate concerns for equality in freight rates, a better balance in industrial development and so on, rather than an unprecedented and direct interference in the business which is professional sport.
There is an old adage in the country that Toronto is a great unifier because Toronto gives everyone in the rest of the country something in common to hate. I think the minister was probably banking on this attitude when he introduced his legislation. I will concede that there is some resentment in my riding of the idea that Toronto is the centre of the world-an idea which was in the mind of the hon. member for York West when, talking about east versus west, he told us this really meant Toronto versus the west; apparently eastern Canada stops at Toronto, excluding every large part of the country. Anyway, I know this opinion of Toronto exists in my part of the country. I regret it. I think the resentment of Toronto is not sufficient reason for embracing legislation which fails to do what it attempts to do, and which sets a very dangerous precedent for direct intervention by government in the field of professional sport.
The single, primary point about this legislation is that it is not going to do what it tries to do. It is not going to be
April 19, 1974

effective. The WFL, whatever the House does, is not suddenly going to dissolve and go away. It is not suddenly going to stop being competitive for Canadian football players on member teams in the CFL. Indeed, it could be argued that the best protection that the CFL has against competition from the WFL is having the Northmen in Toronto, where the guarantees that were given by the sponsors of the Northmen would ensure that there will be an honouring of CFL contracts, that there will not be raiding. John Bassett Jr. has given certain guarantees to the government which would take effect if the Northmen were allowed to continue to function in that city. One was that there would be no raiding, and that would be a great protection to the CFL, a greater protection than is now envisaged in the legislation that has been brought before this House. Then, there has been a guarantee of certain equalization payments to the CFL. There has been a guarantee that no other WFL club would be established within Canadian boundaries, that the franchise rights would be turned over. They are concrete guarantees to the future of the Canadian Football League and will do something, whereas this bill only pretends to do something.
The hon. member for York West (Mr. Fleming), who has now left the chamber, quoted some statements from various officials in western Canada and elsewhere in support of the idea that the minister had articulated in Regina. I think it would be important to add to the record the dates on which that correspondence took place. Because it is my very deep suspicion that that correspondence was sent before the bill was seen; it was sent in support of an idea which would win support in western Canada and elsewhere, but not in support of a piece of legislation which all of us who can read know is not going to be effective in doing what the government says it is trying to do.
It is very clear, and a matter of very great concern to any member of this House who has an interest in professional and amateur football, that the CFL is threatened anyway by the very existence of the World Football League. So long as the WFL exists and is competing, one of two things is going to happen to the CFL, and maybe both. First of all, there is going to be competition for players, which might mean that some of the U.S. imports, who at least add to box office appeal and strengthen CFL teams, will be drawn away; and there is the danger that the quality of football in the CFL will go down, regardless what we do with this bill, unless we can accept and implement the guarantees associated with the establishment of the Northmen in Toronto.
The second thing that could happen is that in this competition for players the CFL would have to bid higher, and consequently it would become more and more difficult for those clubs operating near the profit margin- clubs in western Canada particularly and perhaps the club at Hamilton-to continue to compete. It would be particularly difficult for them to continue to make whatever contribution they are making now to the development and encouragement of amateur football.
I suggest to the House that if there is an aspect of this question that is of legitimate and real concern to those of us here, that aspect is the future of amateur football in this country. It is clear that amateur football receives a certain benefit now from CFL teams who make money
Canadian Professional Football available on a voluntary basis and who also make coaching, films and other assistance available. But it is also obvious that the first people to suffer when there is a decline in the revenue of CFL teams, such as will come from competition with the WFL, will be the amateur teams.
I say again that the one possible protection against that-unless there is to be some new legislation brought in-resides in the guarantees that are associated with the location of the Northmen in Toronto. I hold the view that if there is genuine Canadian football of the kind the minister, in his preamble to the bill, talked about, it is the amateur Canadian football teams. That is where support is needed in this country. If the government is serious about that, and if it does succeed with this bill, maybe-just maybe-it should increase the percentage of Canadian players to 80 per cent, 90 per cent or even 99 per cent. This would be one way of ensuring that there would be effective encouragement of the amateur football associations of this country, whatever happens to the CFL.
Last night the minister indicated there are some other programs that the government intends to follow to encourage amateur football. He indicated that the government had accepted the seven year plan of the Canadian Amateur Football Association and intends to do some other things. I simply want to make it absolutely clear that that undertaking is a separate item from the bill concerning the Northmen. We can presume, unless the minister is involved in some kind of subtle encouragement of support for this bill, that we are going to have support for amateur football anyway, whatever happens to this bill.
Many of us who over the years, in one party or another, have developed an admiration for the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) were struck last night by the very defensive nature of his speech. It was the speech of a man who knows he has made a mistake. He made a long apology for singling out the Northmen, for not acting on those other occasions in professional sport in Canada which have caused harm either directly or by foreclosing possible options for the development of Canadian leagues. He did that by concocting the argument that these other activities, such as baseball, lacrosse, etc., are not Canadian entities anyway. So he is doing nothing about the Expos; he is doing nothing about the fact that foreign owners have to buy the Vancouver Canucks; he is doing nothing to protect lacrosse which suffered a serious blow even during the months that this issue has been before us.
Because this issue has great emotional content the minister also talked about the Grey Cup and how important it is as a national institution. And of course it is. But it is simply false to argue that the Grey Cup will lose its status as a national symbol and event because the Northmen play in Toronto. The Grey Cup has withstood the erosion of broadcasts every Sunday from the National Football League, broadcasts, I might remind the minister, on the Canadian public television network. It has withstood the conversion of the game of football into one that is dependent for its stars and box office appeal primarily upon imports. I say the CFL and the Grey Cup will withstand the Northmen.

April 19, 1974
Canadian Professional Football
The hon. member for York West, if I can return to him for a moment, was eloquent in his early obituary to the CFL, suggesting that this bill before us is the thing, and the only thing, which will keep the CFL in existence. I do not believe, as Russ Jackson, who is a far better authority than I, does not believe, that the CFL is such a fragile plant that it will suddenly wither and die if this piece of ill-considered and ineffective legislation fails to carry in this House.
The minister in his defensive speech last night also spoke at length about the Bassetts, father and son, about what they knew or what they should have known. I suggest the minister's intention was to indicate that the Bassetts knew that the government was going to bring in this kind of legislation, that they knew that the strong arm of the state was going to be brought to bear against them well before they acted. With all respect to the minister, I think that is simply a red herring. Even if the Bassetts did know what the minister and his predecessors had said, and we can only speculate that they did, things ministers say are not law until this parliament makes them law.
I recall, Sir, and I think other members do, that not very long ago the Prime Minister of this country announced a certain skepticism about the work ethic. Is that policy? Will that be law? Will all of us who work be subject to retroactive legislation and two years in jail? I think that indicates the absurdity of the minister's suggestion that because he or his predecessors might have said something that did not then have the force of law, or did not then carry with it the intention of acquiring the force of law, the Bassetts acted in some way that justifies this retroactive legislation against them.
The minister has taken this bad legislation, bad because of the precedents it sets and bad because it does not do what it sets out to do, and he has tried to cloak it in the attractive garb of Canadian nationalism. I mean no offence to the Canadian Football League, but I think that since the minister has made this argument, and since so much of his case depends upon it, and since it has excited the interest and put in jeopardy the seat of his colleague the Minister of State who sometimes is responsible for multiculturalism, I think it might be legitimate to ask how national is the CFL when all of its coaches and nine of its general managers are American born? Most of its stars and most of the people who draw Canadians to the box offices are American born.
The history of the sport and the history of the game that is played in the CFL is a history of change. It started, as my colleague the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Mac-quarrie) pointed out the other night, as a game that is now explicitly excluded from the effects of this legislation by the minister and which has gradually evolved into the game it is today generally along the lines of the U.S. game. It is obvious that the CFL is important to Canada, an important institution as are other of our institutions of national origin, but it is simply misleading to suggest that the Canadian Football League possesses a Canadian identity so distinctive as to be in a place of priority when protecting Canadian culture.

I want to come for a moment to this question of priorities of nationalism and priorities of protecting Canadian identity. Even if this government had turned around and suddenly been seized with the need to protect Canadian identity, why should it start here? Why start with a game dominated by Americans? Why start with football? My colleague, the hon. member for Hillsborough, pointed out the other night that a better place to start would have been by changing the federal immigration laws. If the hon. member for York West were in the House, I would draw to his attention the fact that the federal immigration laws are the responsibility of this government, and this in one thing he cannot fob off on Queen's Park.
The federal immigration laws are the prime reason there is a very serious problem about non-Canadian nationalism in teaching, controlling and hiring in our Canadian universities. Why should football have priority over universities? Why should professional football which does not even directly affect the physical wellbeing and the physical development of Canadian youngsters have a priority over a question which very clearly affects the mentality and attitudinal development of Canadians in universities in this country?
Again on this question of priorities, why do we start with football, with a club owned by Canadians when we continue to allow concessions to Time magazine? Why does football have priority or precedence over Time? Why does football have priority and precedence over book publishing in respect of which the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) has been dithering and dallying, making brave but empty speeches about what he is going to do, yet has done nothing at all? Why is football more important than books?
If football is of such almighty importance, why is there not a policy that will do something about the televising on the Canadian national television network of NFL games every Sunday? If the influence of American football is so rending to our national identity and being, why do we subsidize the CBC to carry NFL football games into Canadian homes for far more Canadians to watch than get into the stadiums, particularly since you cannot get into them in most of the cities in the country? As was pointed out to the minister the other day, if the CBC is carrying these things and we are really concerned about these questions, why do we go to the length of providing French-language translation to carry the NFL into the province of Quebec? Surely, if there were some sense of priority or some sense of context to this action these would be the steps the government would be taking.
I have asked already why, if the minister is worried about developing football as part of Canadian identity, the government is not taking steps now to encourage amateur football in Canada and, indeed, to encourage amateur athletics of all kinds? As an aside, Sir, one of the very great concerns many of us have about this bill that is brought in is a concern which was apparent when the Department of National Health and Welfare began to get involved in fitness and amateur athletic sports. We believe there is a very real role on the side of encouraging Canadian fitness, but the action this government has taken and the priority it has given to professional football has given the caste of nationalism to its activities in sports as being
April 19, 1974

one of preoccupation with professional sports and one of caring not at all or caring enough about amateur athletics. If the Department of National Health and Welfare is to be involved in sports and athletics, then it should be involved on the side of fitness and amateur sports and it should not be long in its acquiring of these priorities and concerns with the professional game.
What is most remarkable of all, Sir, about this legislation and this so-called act to protect and advance Canadian identity, is that it occurs absolutely without any context of national policy. It is not part of a policy at all, it is simply a random strike by the strong arm of the organized state against one venture.
Speaking personally, I believe there are occasions when the state must move in the national interest into fields where it had not been before. I am proud to be part of a party, as was indicated earlier today, which took the initiative to establish the Canadian Wheat Board, and proud to be part of a party which took the initiative to establish the CBC. I believe there is very real room for argument to be made for the state moving from time to time into areas where it had not been before. Once you accept that view you have to go on to say that the state should do that only when it is necessary, as it is not necessary here, and only when the action will be effective, as it will not be effective here, and only when the state knows what it is doing, and I think it is pretty clear that the government of Canada does not know what it is doing with this legislation.
One of the aspects of this bill that worries me most of all as a Canadian who believes there is a legitimate role for state activities and careful watching is that the minister's action today jeopardizes the legitimate principle that the state has some right in activities where the right did not always exist. That right and that principle is jeopardized when the state moves into everything without consistency and without the context of a general policy. It is a very dangerous mentality in a free country that favours governments rushing into every phase of life.
Even if this bill were to be effective, and it is not, there is a legitimate question as to whether the state should suddently swoop into sports, and particularly into professional sports, because professional sports, as we all know if we are honest, are much more entertainment than athletics. This is another kind of business, and that is a question to be considered if this bill is to be effective.
This bill will not be effective. It will not do what it is supposed to do. It is even more dangerous as a precedent of the random intrusion of the strong arm of the state in professional sport. The minister made the point in his remarks that there are no absolutes about whether the state should be in or out of these activities. I happen to believe there are no absolutes about that, but I think the question we must consider all the time is, when does the state become too active. That question is particularly important for those of us who believe that the state does have some legitimate role and who do not want to see that legitimacy destroyed by a random raw exercise of state power without a context of general policy and without a purpose which can be achieved. If we argue that football is
Canadian Professional Football distinctive Canadian culture then this bill is reversing the way we encourage Canadian culture. It is turning it around because the Canadian way is to encourage our own culture positively and not to contort ourselves to keep others out.
That was the principle involved in the establishment of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, in the establishment of the National Film Board and in the establishment of the Canadian Film Development Corporation, which is that we act positively to encourage Canadians. However, if the Lalonde principle is applied to other cultural areas what we would do instead would be to ban circulation of United States movies in Canada, prohibit the circulation of foreign books in Canada and tear up foreign magazines at the border because we are turning around in this legislation the whole long-established Canadian principle of the way in which we encourage identity and self-expression in this country. What we should be doing here, if anything, is encouraging amateur Canadian football and this bill not help that at all. In a free society there are some things the state cannot do.
In Alberta we had experience with that not too long ago in respect of cable television when it was proposed by a former roommate of the Minister of National Health and Welfare that access to cable be prohibited to Calgary and Edmonton. That was designed to protect us against the televised influence of the United States while residents of cities closer to the border in Vancouver and in central Canada were bathed in that influence. This was discriminatory against Alberta. It did not work because it was ineffective as a protection of the Canadian identity. The same kind of inconsistency is evident in a proposal which would allow Torontonians to sit at home and watch United States football on the Canadian National television network or on the United States channels and yet not allow them to go downtown to watch it live. Not only will they not be able to watch the Northmen if this bill passes, but they will not be able to watch the Argos either because they will not be able to get in.
In conclusion, I want to draw attention again to some of the central criticisms with regard to this bill. First, it will not protect the Canadian Football League. The World Football League is an inevitable competitor and its very existence either in Toronto or in some city across the border will create very serious problems of player quality and revenue for teams in the CFL. I repeat this point because I think it is highly important. It may very well prove to be the case that the guarantees associated with the Northmen in Toronto may be the best protection to the CFL as against the inevitable competition from the world Football League. That is point one. This bill will not protect the CFL.
The second point is highly important to all of us concerned about amateur athletics, particularly in the smaller communities. This bill will not protect or encourage amateur football. Indeed it may endanger amateur football and other sports as well because it may give the impression that the government is preoccupied with professional sport rather than with amateur athletics in this country. The third point is that this bill entails an attempt to reverse, to turn right around, the whole approach of developing Canadian culture to an approach of prohibition.

The approach of encouragement is being discarded. The fourth point is that this action is being taken outside the context of national policy. No national policy is involved here. It is simply a random strike by the state against a particular entrepreneur and activity.
Finally, the principles involved in this bill will be a dangerous intrusion by the state, reflecting a dangerous mentality whereby the government might pass retroactive legislation to prohibit anything that it does not much like, an intrusion which threatens to change the entire nature of sport in Canada. The best possible result of this bill would be if the minister would stand in his place and have the courage to say he had made a mistake, that he wanted to do something which perhaps many individuals in Canada wanted to do but that he was not able to devise a bill to achieve what he wanted. The minister should have the humility to say he made a mistake and that he is backing off.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: You are an expert at it.

I perhaps am an expert at humility. I am not sure the minister could make the same claim. He should be prepared to reassess this bill. He should do the right thing which is stand up now and withdraw this bill which will be harmful to professional and amateur football in this country. There is no question that the best way to proceed would be to withdraw this legislation, but if it is not withdrawn then I want it to be clear to the Minister of State and to everybody else that I am against this bill and intend to vote against it.
My party intends to vote against this bill because we think it is dangerous, ineffective legislation and involves principles which will not only reverse the principles and practices in Canada but which will give more force to the idea that the state should intrude at will whether or not it knows what it is trying to do, whether or not the intrusion has any effect and whether or not it is operating in the context of policy.
Mr. Speaker, I intend to oppose this bill and I intend to vote against it.
Hear, hear!

I will summarize the reasons for my view. I think I have about six points on which I will want to expand later. First of all, I say we should not be discussing the issue of football at all at this time when we are faced with the problem of inflation, housing, energy, taxation and a host of other urgent economic and social problems. The hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) reached back into antiquity in his speech. I would say that this is an example of Nero fiddling while Rome burns. My second point is that the parliament of Canada should not be in the business of regulating professional sport at all, and least of all should it be an arbiter between two competing private enterprises.
My third point, and I will expand on it later, is that, in my view at least, the legislation is clearly unconstitutional and beyond the powers of this parliament. My fourth point is that the pretence that this legislation is essential to

defend Canadian culture and unity, to my mind at least, is completely phoney. Canadian culture and unity do not depend upon which of two types of football are played or watched in Canada, and least of all do they depend in the degree of American content in these two particular brands of football. If this is Canadian nationalism, and I say it is not, I want to have none of it.
My fifth point is that a basic right is involved here, that is the right of people to choose for themselves, unless there is some very good reason why they should not be allowed to and such reasons do not exist in the present case, what they want to watch on television or hear on radio. There is no reason why the consumer, that is the viewer who wants to view football directly or through any other means, should not have the widest possible choice, and if that choice involves some degree of American importation- and it does now and will continue to do so-so what? No nationalist rule compels us to say that we are going to shut our doors to seeing things, hearing them and enjoying them because they come from some other part of the world.
Last, and not least, perhaps my reason for opposing this legislation has been said already and I heartily agree with it. This legislation will be completely futile; it will accomplish none of the purposes for which it is designed. I do not regard this matter as being in any sense a party matter. In my party, and no doubt in others, we discuss policy at conventions, at meetings of our council, and in our caucus. We have not done any such thing with regard to this subject. Our caucus has taken the view, and quite rightly in my opinion, that we should be completely free to exercise our own judgment in this matter. I realize that there are strong regional feelings pressuring certain people into the acceptance of this particular type of legislation. I respect their point of view, but I cannot agree with it.
I want to expand on the points I have made. My first point dealt with a proper sense of priorities. I know that the people in my riding in particular, and I have been talking to a good many of them lately, are deeply concerned about the economic crisis that is facing this country. They want action from this parliament in various fields, above all in the field of the high and increasing cost of living. In my own judgment, and that of many people, parliament is demeaned when it departs from these crucial bread and butter issues and spends its time discussing the type of legislation that is presented to us today.
Hear, hear!

The next point I made was that the parliament of Canada should not be in the business of regulating professional sport. I, myself, think that there is an aspect of sport in which the federal government and the federal parliament should be involved, that is the promotion of amateur sport to assist the health, welfare and fitness of the people of this country. I do not believe this legislation adds one iota to the health, welfare and fitness of the people of Canada. If we are going to spend time and money dealing with sport, let us deal with it on that basis and not on the basis that this legislation purports to do.
I say that the legislation is unconstitutional. 1 know very well, as one who has had some experience in constitu-
April 19, 1974

tional law, that it is very hazardous to predict what the result of constitutional decisions in the courts may be. I know that these matters are complex. It is possible to take different points of view. But from the basis of any knowledge I have I say there are at least grave and serious doubts as to whether this parliament has any right to legislate in this field at all. I would have thought that the regulation of sport generally was a matter for the provinces under property and civil rights and a matter of local and private nature.
I do not quite know how this is justified. We have not heard any justification. I heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) make some frivolous replies to questions from the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), but I have not seen, nor have we been vouchsafed any serious analysis as to whether we have the right to deal with it. Does it depend on peace, order or good government, the opening words of section 91? To me that is a nonsensical suggestion. That particular power relates to times of emergency. What emergency requires us to decide whether the Northmen play football in Toronto or do not play football in Toronto?
It might be thought to be justified under the heading of trade and commerce. I know that is a complex subject and there are numerous cases, none of them clear. From my reading I have not been able to discover any case that justifies the suggestion that to allow someone to come across the border to play football, to play a musical instrument, albeit they are playing for money, is a matter of trade and commerce of such dimensions that it would justify legislation here on issues of trade and commerce.
Is it criminal law? Some clauses appear in the bill as if criminal law were included in this bill on purpose. This is an indication of the completely unconstitutional nature of the bill because criminal law certainly is a power that the federal government has but it cannot be used to justify interference in a field where the government has no right to be.

Mr. Speaker, I was giving an outline of the various reasons why I think this bill should be opposed. One of the reasons was that I thought it was beyond the constitutional power of this parliament to pass, and I touched on some of the headings under which it might be
Canadian Professional Football sought to be justified. I mentioned the subject of criminal law which, of course, is within the power of parliament. But, Mr. Speaker, I find the references to penalties in this bill clearly colourable. One just cannot attach a penalty to a bill which is dealing with something that is basically provincial and, as a result, call it criminal law.
I do not think criminal law has any part in dealing with the question of who plays what sort of football, or who watches what sort of football. I cannot imagine that that subject has anything whatsoever to do with the field of criminal law. I find the suggestion that perhaps it is justified under this heading is clear evidence of the lack of any proper basis of constitutional support, and indeed is a clear indication that this legislation is colourable legislation.
Some people may ask why bother about the constitution these days? Some people do not seem to be very interested in or to bother much with constitutional matters. I particularly ask the government members, some of whom have been stout defenders of provincial rights, why are they so silent with respect to this intrusion in the field of provincial rights? I myself have never been a strong defender of provincial rights because I felt that, as a federal member of parliament, my main interest was concerned with defending the federal rights of this parliament. But I think we need balance.
To me it is a most extraordinary thing that a whole political party-so far as I know not a single one has got up here to protest against this bill-has been silent on this invasion of the provincial sphere. Could it possibly be because the bill in the first instance is aimed at the area of Toronto, at the province of Ontario? Do they think provincial rights are important when they concern some other province, but not worth defending if they concern this particular area of the country?
I want to warn people who think like this that if they can invade the field of provincial rights using the flimsy pretext of this bill, then they can invade those rights tomorrow in a different sphere affecting different areas of the country. As I say, the silence of the government party on this issue is astounding and astonishing to me.
My next point is this: I do not believe that the pretence that this bill is a defence of Canadian culture and Canadian unity has any substance. I have described it as phony, and I cannot think of a better word. We are all Canadian nationalists and we all recognize the importance of maintaining the identity and self confidence of Canada. There are many fields in which we need more Canadian nationalism. We need it in the defence of our resources, in the development of our resources, and we need it particularly in international affairs. All too often we have borrowed our ideas from other countries, first from Great Britain and, currently, the United States. I believe in the strength and independence of Canada and, although nationalism is not the ultimate loyalty, I still think it is very important.
But how is it that a game which is at least semi-American, professional football, has suddenly become the symbol of Canadian nationalism. If that is the symbol of Canadian nationalism, I say Canadian nationalism is pretty sick. If we have to borrow, as our symbol, a game

which everybody who knows anything about it will admit is thoroughly Americanized, if we have to borrow that and defend that as the symbol of our nationalism, our nationalism is in a pretty poor state.
If one concedes that somehow or other Parliament must insist on Canadian sports remaining Canadianized, what were we doing when a genuine Canadian sport, lacrosse, was taken over by the Americans. No one can deny that lacrosse was a basic Canadian institution. Is the football that is played part of our culture, when a large proportion of our players are American and rules are the same as American rules? When the forward pass was introduced in the United States, it was introduced in Canada as well only a few weeks or months afterwards. Our so-called Canadian football is a derivation of American football. Even if it was not so originally, it has become so over the course of years.
There are forms of nationalism which are just. It is perfectly reasonable to require a certain Canadian content in what goes over our air waves. I do not object to that, for what goes over our air waves is closely related to our culture and nationality. But I deny that this particular form of football, this professional football which we are discussing, is such a national symbol.
I read the recital to this bill. It spoke of national unity. All the noble words were used in it. I have never before seen such a ridiculous recital to a bill. If I were to bring a bill forward with that sort of recital in it, I would be ashamed of myself.
Another point I made is this: people have the right to choose what they shall see and view, and what sort of entertainment they want to watch. This right belongs to everybody, not just to people in the Toronto area. It will be a sorry day when Parliament gets into the business of trying to regulate what we can see.
Hear, hear!

True, the right to choose is not absolute. At times it must be interfered with for the benefit of the public generally. As I say, it is not ah absolute right. But I fail to see what circumstances has suddenly come about which gives the government the right to tell people, in effect, that they cannot watch a football player who happens to be affiliated with some foreign league. I would deny the government this right. Although it is not covered in the Bill of Rights, this involves a basic human right, and you should not interfere with it unless you have a very good reason. I do not see any such reason in this particular case.
Another point I made is that the present legislation is doomed to futility. It just will not work. This point has already been expounded in the House and I will not spend long on it. I see no reason for believing that this legislation will achieve the purpose at which it is aimed, the protection of the Canadian Football League. They would be far better protected if they accepted the proposals made by the proponents of the WFL, that there be no raiding. If they insist on throwing the other league out of the country altogether, they cannot appeal to them. They cannot ask them to desist from raiding, from using their superior financial resources to diminish the quality of Canadian football. If they are thrown out, how is that going to help

Canadian football? This bill is a weapon. It is a weapon which should not be used at all, for the end that it purports to achieve it obviously will not achieve. Therefore, it is futile.
I have had and have a great deal of respect for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. His is an extremely important portfolio. So far as I know, he is carrying out his duties well. I say to him, this bill is an aberration. It is tragic that a man with his reputation has come forward and associated his name with this sort of aberration. I have no desire to prolong this debate. Let me summarize the reasons why I say we should vote against this bill. First, it is an unwarranted interference with freedom of choice. It is an invasion of the provincial field of property and civil rights. It is outside the constitutional power of the federal government. Its pretended defence of Canadian nationalism, unity and culture is without substance. It is not a matter of high priority in the present day of crisis. Lastly, it will be futile for carrying out the purpose for which it appears to be aimed. For these reasons I appeal to all members of the House, irrespective of party, to repudiate this particularly bad legislation.

The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) wondered what my position would be, as I come from Saskatchewan. The Treasury Board has just received word that the air traffic controllers will go on strike at midnight, on Sunday, and here we are, arguing whether we should protect the monopoly of the Toronto Argonauts, the team the people watch in the Toronto area. What is all this nonsense? The country is saddled with strikes. The railways are 56 million bushels behind in grain deliveries. People in the world are starving because we cannot deliver wheat to export position, and we talk about football. If inflation goes above 10 per cent and if half the traffic in the country is stalled, will we talk about tennis? Taking the argument to ridiculous lengths, when inflation reaches 15 per cent, will the government bring in a bill to regulate ping pong?
One wonders about this government. When I go to my constituency, people ask why we cannot have legislation which deals with the Criminal Code and abortion. I tell them there are 30 departments of government and everyone is either trying to update their legislation or bring in new legislation to meet the ever-increasing demands of the public. How will I ever be able to explain to my constituents why we had to spend several days debating

football? Over the years I have sent requests to the department asking for financial support for people honestly engaged in the promotion of amateur sports. The answers have always been the same, we get nothing. However, the minister is going to spend $18 million this year and $25 million by 1975-76. Where is it going to go? I did not like it at first, but after seeing nothing else, it kind of grew on me. The CBC could not carry Canadian games so we had to watch American ball. Now, the government is getting kind of fussy about what kind of ball there may be in Toronto.
It seems the department of fitness and health can give grants to Lethbridge and Montreal. The people in my constituency contributed to support Expo '67 and the great monuments and facilities that remain there. Olympics '76 will also cost the Canadian taxpayer. However, we do not get anything in the rural and sparsely populated areas. North Battleford in my constituency was going to host the Canadian senior baseball championships this year. When we hosted the Saskatchewan winter games, we requested some television coverage by the state-owned CBC. They said they could not go there and do that, yet they spent $25 million sending progress reports on sports events in Mexico. Why do they not have money to project happenings that are taking place in remote areas, as I suppose the government considers them to be, like North Battleford? Facilities will be required to host these games in Kinders-ley and Unity. It will not be possible to get any financial assistance from the minister's department.
There is talk about football being part of the Canadian culture. I have not received one single letter on this issue. I did receive a booklet from the Canadian Football League which is not looking very far down the road when supporting this legislation. I quote from that paper:
-Canadian Clubs would lose just as much or more money but more importantly they will have lost 100 years of Canadian sporting tradition.
They say it will not only wipe out the Canadian Football League, but all sporting tradition in Canada. What nonsense. They further state:
The Grey Cup Game, as one of Canada's greatest annual events, will disappear with it-
No one is talking about the disappearance of the CFL. This bill does not guarantee the Saskatchewan Rough Riders will survive in Regina. Whether or not Saskatchewan continues to have a football team will depend on the ability of those managing the team to sell their product. This bill to keep a football team out of Toronto and support the monopoly of the Argonauts in that city will not do anything for Regina, Calgary or Edmonton. You do not get excellence in sport by eliminating the better players. Look at what the Americans have done to promote hockey in their country. They could simply say they will not allow any Canadian hockey players into the United States. We know what the result would be. There would not be a team in St. Louis or Cleveland. There would not be two hockey teams in New York or Boston. Without excellence in sports, you just do not get spectators. A person will pay $100 to see two excellent boxers but will not walk across the street to see two mediocre ones. This socialistic minister is trying to promote mediocracy in sports as well as everything else.
The minister's speech made it quite clear why we are debating this issue today. The government is hanging by a thread not knowing what to do. What do you do in a case like that? You find some filler legislation. The minister said, as recorded at page 1566 of Hansard, and I quote:
As a matter of fact, although we consider this a matter of significance we do not consider it a matter of confidence.
Why is it here? Why are we debating it? They sense an election in the near future. As the minister said at page 1561, it is an emotional issue, a gut issue. That is why we are debating it. The government cannot be defeated on it. It is an emotional issue, but they are trying to gain the support of Canadians for it.
I live in a town of about 3,000 people. We have local hockey teams. They have done something to promote unity. In the last three years, they travelled to Powell River, B.C. and Bathurst, New Brunswick. They went to the Canadian finals intermediate A hockey, real amateur hockey. These fellows do not get paid fancy salaries. They play for pleasure and to entertain the local people. They live in sparsely populated areas and are hard pressed for money. We produce a lot for the economy of this country in terms of grain and cattle, but we are denied any support from this minister's department. I requested some support when the Rosetown Red Wings had to travel to St. John, New Brunswick, to play in the intermediate A finals. There was no support in terms of travel expenses or help to have these games broadcast in Rosetown and surrounding area.
If football is a traditional part of Canadian culture, certainly hockey is much more so. I would not hesitate to guess that for every child with a football, there are a thousand children with a hockey stick. The minister made a speech at the University of Lethbridge on awards night. He said that Canada was not winning gold medals at the Olympics and countries with populations smaller than ours were winning more medals. He said we want to help the best Canadian athletes in their pursuit of excellence.

How does the bill achieve either of these objectives? I do not see how keeping the Northmen out of Toronto is likely to help us win more gold Olympic medals. I do not see that it will help our athletes achieve any greater excellence. It is difficult for socialists to understand excellence, to understand that mankind has always

Mr. Speaker, I am in some difficulty, I must confess, in finding within the lexicon of the English language words to describe the emotion I feel as I stand up here to debate this over-poweringly important measure. My thoughts stray to my riding, not 2,000 yards west of here. I think of the young housewife whose husband, by whom she has had three children, earns less than $10,000 a year, and of the tiny, tiny tender smile that must flit over her lips as she delves deeply into her handbag in an effort to make a down payment on the weekend groceries, and remembers that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has made Toronto safe for the Argonauts. I think of the many hundreds of thousands of people-507,000 by the government's own count last Monday-who are out of work in this country and who, as they line up to receive their unemployment cheques, may be taking real comfort from the fact that the WFL shall not pass.
A thousand laid off last week in my city.

Last Monday, the increases in the cost of living were announced. As we all know, the average increase in the consumer price index for the year was 10.1 per cent. In some cities it was as high as 12.5 per cent for the year with St. John's leading the pack. In Ottawa, where the minister sits five days a week, it was 11.4 per cent, the monthly increase being .9 per cent. This is in addition to the multiplicity of other disasters which have been brought on the heads of the unsuspecting and undeserving people of this country as a result of the really creative incompetence of the government.
As I say, I find myself at a loss for words to describe my feelings. Certainly, "honoured" is not the word. "Happy" does not describe the way I feel, either. What I really feel is demeaned and deceived and put upon at having to sit here and watch this kind of spectacle. I think of all the people in the Public Service who are trying through their collective bargaining agents to get a decent collective agreement out of the Treasury Board, and not succeeding. I think of all the travellers who find themselves waiting at airports, unable to reach their destinations. I think of the many people waiting for mail, including a bunch of postal employees in Kentville, Nova Scotia who went on strike because they could not get their pay cheques because the post office employees are on strike elsewhere, as a result of which their cheques could not get to Kentville.
The firemen at the airports across the country want to vote on their contract, but once again they cannot because

the post office is on strike and they cannot receive their ballots. Even if they did succeed in getting their ballots on the plane, they had better vote fast because the air traffic controllers are going to be on the street by midnight Sunday. In the midst of all this the government brings on this extraordinary measure to regulate in what fashion, in what numbers, and by whom, a leather spheroid shall be propelled up and down a 100 yard field.
At this point I should like to read a charming editorial that appeared in this morning's Globe and Mail entitled "Canada crowds in again". I think it is particularly poignant in the context of this moment. It goes like this:
It is said that Barbados can bestow a special sense of tranquility on all who visit it; a calming, benign influence that can waft troubles away on zephyr breezes. We trust it worked its therapeutic wonders on Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau during the five or six days he spent there, because he returns to an in-tray that threatens to break the legs of his desk.
If I can interpolate a personal observation here, those of us who have been unfortunate enough to have to witness the ill temper of the aforesaid member from Barbados know full well that there is no discernible evidence that the tranquility or zephyr breezes had any ameliorating effect on his temper at all. To continue:
Some of us can go on holiday and return to find that our week has been invisibly mended. Hardly anyone noticed we were gone, and events just lumbered easily along. It doesn't work that way for prime ministers.
Then, it poses this rhetorical question:
From calypso to collapso? Well, we can't be sure what lurks behind the enigmatic smile of New Democratic Party Leader David Lewis or behind the doors of the Conservative caucus room, but staying afloat in Ottawa can be more fun than skindiving in the Caribbean.
The first thing Mr. Trudeau should understand is that if his in-tray is overburdened, it is not the fault of the Post Office. That operation has done all that could be expected of it to ease the flow of communication by letter.
Let him be thankful also that the possibility of intrusion on his working day by delegations from all parts of the country has been thoughtfully reduced through a gift by airport firefighters, with air traffic controllers standing by. In keeping with the fiesta spirit that goes with labour's rites of spring, the St. Lawrence River pilots have made their own unique contribution.
Canada is wonderful in the springtime. It's nature's time of renewal and all around us things are pushing merrily upward-wages, prices- you name it. Yes, inflation is another of those little things that tells you you have been away. Even in six days you can see the index move.
Lay a budget on us. Give us something to sing and dance about. The good old countervailing force, remember? We have it on the highest authority that this will be a good budget, and those of us who didn't make it to Barbados this winter need a glimpse of sunshine.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if we have not got sunshine, at least we have football. In an earlier reincarnation the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) once functioned as principal secretary to the Prime Minister. In that lofty capacity he had occasion to speak to a seminar of Liberal party workers on the west coast. This particular seminar had to do with the participation of party workers in the formation of Liberal party policy. He said at this seminar: "Of course, you have to realize that none of these policy resolutions are binding; after all you are only a few per cent". So they said to him: "What if you have more than a few per cent? What if you have 51 per cent, or even 100 per cent of all the workers in the Liberal party deciding we should do something that you did not want to do?" "Well," he replied, "we would send our P.R. men out to do
Canadian Professional Football a better selling job because we would realize that we had made a mistake".
If I ever saw concrete evidence that that curious attitude toward the democratic process has not changed one bit, it is the almost inch think folder of profession "bumph" that came our way in trying to sell this dubious proposition to members of parliament. We have received telegrams from mayors, and following a rhetorical question posed this morning by the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark), I should like to tell the minister that of all the telegrams and letters received from mayors of various cities in this country, only three were written after March 1, out of about 15, by the look of it. One has to assume, since the bill was recently introduced in this House, that they knew not what it contained, unless the minister was sliding around showing it to them in advance, and I can scarcely credit that. So I think we can take these letters, telegrams and all the rest with a grain of salt.
As far as the letters are concerned, I should like to read a couple of them to the minister. One from a constituent of mine says this:
I would like to list a few of the reasons why I think Mr. Lalonde is being ridiculous in his stand.
-The Northmen have guaranteed that the equalization from the
Argonauts would not decrease from last season's level for the next
three years.
Actually, it is the next ten years.
They also hold refusal rights to another WFL team in Canada and have guaranteed the government they will not allow another team to play in Canada.
Mr. Lalonde's worry about Canadian sport comes much too late for anybody to seriously believe that is his only motive and not a vote-getter from the western provinces ...
If the government is really worried about the CFL going belly-up why don't they set up a grant system for the leagues teams that are not drawing large enough crowds to support them. The manner in which the government is spending money and giving grants to the most idiotic causes would suggest this would be a worthy cause.
This is a letter to the minister from a constituent of mine who was kind enough to send me a copy:
Canadians have more faith in their institutions and themselves than you give them credit for. Normal competition leads to strength and vitality-government interference leads to complacency and decay.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, a letter that appeared a couple of days ago in the Ottawa Journal from an admirable person who signs himself or herself "K. C. Shindler":
Sirs:
Our federal government has strange priorities. The cost of living has gone up 10.4 per cent in one year, vegetable prices will go up between 20 and 30 per cent by next autumn, Agriculture Minister Eugene Whelan wants higher beef prices in Canada, and now Health Minister Marc Lalonde has introduced a bill to protect the CFL from the WFL.
How about a bill to protect me from the federal government?
Why don't you table the letter?

Here it is, any time you want it. I should just like to comment on some of the remarks made during the minister's lengthy and paranoid apologia for this curious position of his last night. He said, as reported at page 1561 of Hansard:
We hear about the principles of free enterprise and free competition in the marketplace.
