Fancy that.
We are told that the state should not interfere with private business unless, of course, private business requests state help. We are bombarded with lectures about people's freedom of choice and freedom of movement and other fundamental rights.
I suggest that must be an imposition on the government. Imagine being bombarded with speeches about people's rights! This entitles them to take a long, long second look at this bill. Just imagine-freedom of choice and freedom of rights are being urged upon the government. How uncomfortable it must make them feel. The minister goes on to say that there is nothing unprecedented or arbitrary in the government's position.
I ask hon. members to consider precisely what it is that this bill does. It makes it a criminal offence, punishable by up to two years behind bars and/or a fine which is set at whatever a court deems advisable, if a person decides to set up a particular business in Canada, to employ American nationals and to carry on part of that business in the United States. That is exactly what the bill does, no less.
Is there another industry to which this applies? Is there another area of entrepreneurship in which a person risks going to jail and/or a fine of undetermined size because he decides to hire as his employees people who come from countries other than Canada, and because he decides to carry on business at least part of the time in another country? I do not believe so. As for being arbitrary, Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is a fashion in which you could behave more arbitrarily than by threatening someone with two years behind bars, unless it is to threaten him with a sentence of death. I think on this basis the minister's defence of this position fails to stand up at all.
Then, he goes on to appeal to the basest kind of prejudice when he says that those whose manufacturing industries have been protected in the past by tariff legislation should not complain about this. He finds that terribly ironic and he tried to suggest to us that this is a quid pro quo on the part of the whole of eastern Canada because of a reasonable position taken in bargaining over the price of oil by western provinces. I suggest to you that this is just about as strained a comparison as the bit of gibberish that came out of the minister of state for multiculturalism this morning when he was insisting on bellowing across whether the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark) was in favour of Canadian unity. I agree with the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) that if the issue of whether John Bassett or Fred Schmertz, or whoever, is going to be allowed to operate a football team in Toronto in competition with the Toronto Argonauts bears heavily on the issue of national unity, then this country is in worse shape than I had imagined it to be.
This issue of national unity has been a stalking horse of this particular brand of Grits for far too long now. In the first session of this House after the election of 1972 we heard them get on the national unity hobby horse and, in the person of their Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and national leader, accuse even the leader of this party of racism during the election campaign of October 1972, and accuse this entire political party of damaging the concept of national unity. They were rebuffed at that time quite

properly and they will be turned back and rebuffed on this issue if they try to make out that this is important to national unity, any more important than mom's apple pie. Perhaps they will come back in here with another imagined threat to national unity in the near future, but they certainly have not made any point here at all.
As to whether this team, the Toronto Northmen, would be a threat to the Canadian Football League, and this is the unifying premise of the bill, I want to examine this with you. I would be very, very grateful if the minister or anybody else over there could tell me precisely how this team located in Toronto is going to damage anybody. The existence of the WFL itself is going to threaten not only the Canadian Football League but the National Football League in the United States because there will be unrestrained raiding and bidding for services. Indeed, this very day in the newspaper John Bassett claims to have signed Larry Uteck, the Toronto Argonauts' first pick of the Canadian college draft. That kind of thing is going to go on apace. The very existence of that league, with its need for players, is going to put the pressure on every other professional football league in North America, and it is not going to matter a hoot in hell whether that team is located in Toronto, Nashville, North Carolina or wherever it is they propose to locate if they are turned out of Toronto. It is the existence of the league that is a threat, and, despite what the minister would like to do, we cannot legislate the league out of existence; we can only knock out one of its teams, and even then we can only push that across the border. It will not make one iota of difference to the Saskatchewan Roughriders, the Edmonton Eskimos, the Vancouver Lions or any other team if that team is allowed to operate out of Toronto.
It is the league itself that threatens, if indeed there is much of a threat, and I do not think there is because it has been the experience with professional sport of any kind, particularly professional football, that the more people who are exposed to the sport the higher the number will be at the box office. Today, in fact, the United Press International has reported out of Washington:
The Federal Communications Commission reported yesterday the lifting of the home game television blackout by Congress last season had little if any impact on the mounting prosperity of professional football, which enjoyed its best year in 1973.
"The anti-blackout law appears to have had minimal impact on the 26 member teams of the National Football League in its first season of operation," a report issued by the FCC read. "It is unlikely that season-ticket sales will be adversely affected by the law because there seems to be an excess demand for tickets.
"In fact, 1973 was the best season ever for the NFL-"
That simply means that a great many more people are turning out to NFL games despite the fact that they can see them in their own homes on television in some cities because they are being exposed to the game, a great many converts are being made and they want to see them in person. The same thing is true of Canadian football and of Canadian hockey. Whenever you expose more people to a sport everybody benefits.
I suggest the very same will be true of Toronto where there is a market of up to four million people. You can not buy a season-ticket in that stadium and you have not been able to in the last 10 years. You are lucky if you can get standing room even when they are losing, and that is most

of the time. I should know having been an Argonaut fan until I moved down to Ottawa, and I cannot even get tickets to the games here.
Let us consider what the Toronto Northmen have offered to pay. They have offered to pay the difference between the equalization grants, paid principally by the Argonauts to western teams, if they need it; the difference between what was paid under that heading in 1973 and any loss experienced by the Toronto Argonauts in earnings at the box office for the next 10 years. They have offered to restrict their television broadcasting to local TV; they have offered a no-raiding clause of teams in the CFL and have stressed that they will urge upon their colleagues in the WFL the same no-raiding agreement.
I ask you to consider what is going to happen if the Northmen are barred from Toronto. There will, of course, be the absence of a no-raiding agreement. They will be free to raid, and they have already started to do this. There will be absolutely no prohibition on all of the teams in the WFL from raiding the sources from which the CFL customarily gets its American imports, and we must bear in mind that all the CFL teams have a very high proportion of Americans on their payrolls. They are getting these players from the U.S. college draft and from American teams in the NFL, and now they are going to have a powerful and well financed component to bid in all in the same fields in the same places.
Unfortunately salaries are going to rise for a couple of years and everybody is going to feel the pressure. Unfortunately, the quality of play will decline because talent is going to be diluted. That happened in the NHL which is just starting to get a little better. Football leagues in both countries are going to feel the effects of the WFL and there is no mistake about that. The World Football League will continue to exist and will continue to be in opposition to the Canadian Football League regardless of what this parliament does.
I would suggest to you that what we are being asked to do here is accept a law which is pure, political protectionism, which is legislation in restraint of trade, which has as I said earlier dubious legality and constitutionality and which is a very thinly disguised attempt on the part of the federal government to do under the guise of criminal law what it could never do in civil law because of provincial jurisdiction.
We are being asked to do this at a time when more than half a million people are out of work, at a time when inflation is at an all-time high, at a time when the country is very close to being paralyzed by strikes in the public sector due to this government's incompetency, and at a time when this government has been discredited from coast to coast in the public view and would not continue to exist were it not refusing daily to submit to a test of confidence in this House.
Despite all the sophistry that floats across the floor to any member unfortunate enough to differ with the spurious arguments of the Liberal Party, despite all the sophistry about "Let us pass it now," I will say once again to the government that until the happy day when the voters of this country have a chance to express their views at the
Canadian Professional Football ballot box you-as disgusting a prospect as it may be for most-are the government, and if you bring in bad legislation in this House you need not expect the opposition parties to lie down before you and let you roll over them and enact bad law. And that is all this bill is.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks this afternoon will be very short because I would be pleased to allow this matter to go to a vote as soon as possible. Indeed, the only reason I rise to speak is to express my shock and the shock of my constituents at the decision of the government to introduce this legislation affecting football as a means of disguising its abject failure to deal with the pressing social and economic problems facing this country.
Last night I indicated my concern about the failure of the government to take any action to deal with the explosion of housing costs in Canada today. I was shocked, and remain shocked, that the only recent action by the government was to further drive up interest rates and to put the cost of housing even further beyond the reach of the average Canadian. The government is not presenting any more speakers to defend its flimsy case for second reading of this bill. They have obviously received the same response from their constituents as members of parliament on this side of the House have received, namely, that the parliament of Canada should be dealing not with frivolous legislation about football but with measures to come to grips with the host of crises facing this country.
I am intrigued that hon. members opposite claim we should hurry this legislation through to committee. All of us on this side would be delighted to do so if the government had any legislation to present dealing with the problems facing Canadians. In Canada today we have more than a 10 per cent rate of inflation. Where is the government's budget that we have been demanding? The government cannot even give us a date for the budget. The cost of housing increased by 41.8 per cent in Toronto in the last year. Torontonians are demanding legislation, not to tell them what football teams they can watch but how they can own a home.
The Unemployment Insurance Commission is in disarray. Where is the legislation to deal with that problem? Half a million Canadians are without work at the present time. What does the government plan to do to deal with that situation? There are strikes at our airports, in our mail system and on our lakes. What action is the government taking to deal with these problems?
They are probably getting ready to stop the railways.

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) says the government is probably getting ready to stop the railways now, too. If the government were prepared to introduce legislation that would deal with these matters, all of us on this side would gladly sit down. But we know, the government knows and the people of Canada know that the government has no program to present to parliament and that any legislation we will see after this bill goes to committee will be strictly housekeeping legisla-

April 19, 1974
Canadian Professional Football
tion. It will not deserve, and it will not obtain, the attention of the press or of the Canadian people.
Instead, the government is carefully preparing a well orchestrated, three-ring circus of witnesses for the committee, thinking at the same time that no one will be able to say the time of the House of Commons is being taken up by this silly bill because it will be in committee. In other words, the effect of this legislation is only that of a red herring the object of which is to distract public attention from the failure of the government to deal with the real problems facing Canadians today. I repeat, if the government has any legislation to present to cope with the high cost of housing or with the chaos caused by strikes, or if it has a budget to present, I will sit down now and my colleagues also will be silent.
What has been the record of this government? It was the intention of the government that we should not be here this week, that the problems of Canadians should not be discussed in parliament at this time. When we demanded that, as a condition of parliament's recessing, members of parliament should at least have a day this month or early next month to deal with the government's handling of the economy, the government refused because it knows it has lost the confidence of the parliament of Canada and the people of Canada and it is determined to cling to power with all its force.
When we refused to allow government members their holiday, what did the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) do? He flew off to Barbados. I was interested on Tuesday to read the article which appeared on page 9 of the Globe and Mail dealing with the Prime Minister's reaction to this particular problem. The final paragraph of the article reads as follows:
A spokesman for Mr. Trudeau said the Prime Minister, who left for Barbados on Friday with his family, would probably return to Ottawa either today or Wednesday-in time for health minister Lalonde's controversial football bill.
In other words, in the opinion of the Prime Minister and of his discredited government, the government's handling of the economy is not important enough to bother with, but this fraudulent football bill justifies the Prime Minister's return to Canada.
What is the attitude of the cabinet, the people who are supposed to be running this country? During the question period today, 60 per cent of them were missing, including the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang). I am delighted that today the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) is gracing us with his presence. As we look at the treasury benches now we find that of the 29 members of the cabinet who should be here, two are present. And these do not include the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) or his parliamentary secretary.
Shame.
They are out blowing up the football.

This is a government that is leaderless and directionless, a government that was repudiated by the people of nine of

the ten provinces, and of both territories; a government that has the sight and the smell of decay about it. Nothing more graphically demonstrates its distorted sense of priorities in its last days than this legislation.
Mr. Speaker, the government says it wants to protect Canadian culture and Canadian athletics, although only yesterday the Minister of National Health and Welfare admitted on television that this bill will not save the CFL, that it is no panacea. In fact, there is even evidence to suggest that it will damage the CFL by encouraging American WFL teams to raid their lower-paying Canadian counterparts. I think it is worth remembering, when the government wraps itself in the robes of Canadian nationalism and takes measures to protect football, that our national sport in Canada is not football and it is not hockey; it is lacrosse which was first played here by our Canadian Indians.
I come from a town in which lacrosse has been played for generations. I invite the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who has now returned to the House, to talk to the people who play lacrosse and learn from them what assistance they have been receiving from the government and from his department. There has been precious little help, if any, for our national sport. As my colleague from Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) pointed out last night, there is the prospect of our losing the game of lacrosse to the Americans as teams are created in the United States and there is virtually no assistance available for the sport from our federal government.
Last summer I wrote the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) and the minister responsible for Information Canada, pointing out the importance of promoting this part of our national heritage. I was informed that the government's promotional efforts amounted to one 14-minute film produced in 1964, another produced in 1965, and a booklet on lacrosse in Canada. What a bold initiative!
Mr. Speaker, last year I had an opportunity to watch the Grey Cup game in Toronto. I could not help but have the feeling, watching these two corporations play against each other, that it is very similar to watching the struggle between General Motors and Ford. Unlike the minister, however, I do not begrudge people watching football if they wish, whether it is played by the Toronto Northmen or by the Toronto Argonauts. As individuals, they should have this opportunity. But I cannot help getting the feeling that the ultimate good of the country will be decided, not by professional athletics but by amateur athletics which have been neglected by the government. I see the minister nods his head; he is in agreement.

repeat that this is not the time for smokescreen legislation from a dying government. This is not the time for inaction on national issues. It is the time for an honest attempt to deal with our real problems. I am afraid that such an
April 19, 1974

honest attack on our problems is more than we can expect from this government.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I note that some members are eager to refer this bill to the committee, but I think there is much to be said about it. As for myself,
I am particularly interested in Bill C-22 now under consideration.
My interest is quite natural since I spent some years practising various sports, namely hockey, baseball and football. The latter is not unfamiliar to me, on the contrary, because I had the opportunity to follow closely and particularly the sports practised in Canada. The motivation which can be instilled into young people in connection with sports generally deserves special attention.
I find it strange, though, that members of the party sponsoring this bill be absent or remain silent because I know, especially since I come from the province of Quebec, that thousands of sports fans, especially football fans, are following the debates on this bill. From the outset, we were asked to limit the number of speeches, so that the bill might be referred to the committee and that the House might deal with more important problems.
Mr. Speaker, it is quite unbecoming on the part of the government party to tell us that we are delaying the debates and wasting the time of this House because we have been saying for two months to the government that we do not want this legislation.
The hon. member himself is now delaying the debate, not us.

Exactly, Mr. Speaker; the hon. member who has just interrupted me should then rise and speak right now.
We are being blamed for delaying the debates whereas we have been warning for two months the responsible minister and the government not to bring forward such a meaningless legislation. Mr. Speaker, the government has no business interfering in such an area.
And they will try to make the public believe that the Official Opposition party is wasting the time of this House, when we are calling upon the government to introduce specific measures dealing with today's problems.
I wonder, for instance, whether it is not government strategy to put forward a bill about football, in order to hide basic problems our society is faced with, such as the strike that is presently under way throughout the country. Members of Parliament are invited to speak about football in order to prevent the public from realizing the failure of the government to find solutions for several months, Mr. Speaker.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, I really wanted to speak about this legislation because I am interested in sports in general. I think I can say that I have some knowledge in the whole field of sports. I think it is not exaggerated to add that putting forward a bill about football under the pretence that this is the only way of saving Canadian
Canadian Professional Football football and getting thousands of young Canadians to be interested in it, is a phoney assertion. The provisions of this bill certainly do not deserve the support of most hon. members. What is the reason for such a bill? They claim that it will foster national unity. I wonder what is the relation between that concept and football. God knows how many times we failed in respect of a great many problems a lot more important than this one.
Now they are talking about economic nationalism. A number of speakers have already urged the Minister to take more concrete steps, in the industrial area, for example, so that Canadians may own a majority of shares. In my opinion, the government should introduce measures to encourage Canadians to invest in Canadian industries, so that they may feel they are the real owners of this country's resources.
When we introduced such a bill, you voted against it.
The hon. member should keep his ears open and his mouth shut!

I do not think there is enough legislation fostering economic nationalism, but the government should not make us laugh. While a number of hon. members have cracked jokes which were apparently aimed at reviling members of the government but which only succeeded in making us laugh, surely the Canadian public must wonder why the government introduced such legislation which affects one particular sport only.
You are saying this, not the Canadian public.

Mr. Speaker, I will later make some revealing comments to the minister.
If he wants us to promote Canadian football, there is not one member in this House who is against giving direct support to Canadian football. I am the first one to promote this sport and I wish a law were passed to ensure that most if not all owners of these teams were Canadians. I also wish to see any possibility of competition banned in football. But I will not accept to see young Canadians deprived of motivation to achieve excellence, to better themselves in a professional sport, whether football or hockey.
The minister has stated that football is in danger. But I have here a paper that sheds light on this, which has precisely been issued by his department. And I quote: "Football is in danger". In fact, Mr. Speaker, all sports are in danger.
We talk about the importance of participation, about the quality of football players. Why don't we talk about participation in all sports, about the quality of hockey or baseball players as well as players in any other sport. That is just as important as the opportunities offered to young people by Canadian football. And why should it not be so for all other sports?
The problem in the area of football in particular will not be solved through this legislation, which is totally inade-

April 19, 1974
Canadian Professional Football quate and even unfair. I fail to see how the government could justify itself by saying that Canadian football can be promoted through such legislation.
I have here a document signed by Mr. Jean-Paul Char-trand of Montreal which says: The Minister of National Health and Welfare is not helping the Montreal Alouettes. In Ontario, football is a great deal better organized than in Quebec where it is almost nonexistent at the serious amateur level. One look at the Alouettes line up is enough to find out that our best Canadian players are not home grown, unless they attended an American college.
There is talk of actually encouraging our young people to play Canadian football. But I regret that all sports in Canada have not been included and it is certainly not necessary to pass a legislation to keep a foreign league or team from settling in this country, when this would be the only opportunity for our young people of being offered sound competition with all the advantages that this carries.
Until now funds allotted to amateur sport have been entirely restricted to a few super stars, some of whom have benefited from scholarships. What has been done for kids in grade school or high school? It is at this level that an amateur sport policy must truly be initiated. The present policy is altogether inadequate. It is not by passing legislation on football that we would remedy these anomalies. What is keeping the minister from allotting funds to our universities in order that our football players may develop in a normal way as they have the right to?
So the government's problem lies not in the need to pass a piece of legislation but in the inadequacy of the funds allotted to amateur sport while the Canadian policy in that respect is altogether inadequate and even absurd. What is required, as I have already mentioned, is the establishment, in consultation with the provinces, of a department of sports and recreation which would be responsible for physical conditioning in Canada. This will help solve many problems, besides encouraging young people to play not only football but all the other sports in which they are interested provided they are qualified to participate in them. So, this participation and the quality of the players to which reference is made in this bill make it totally unacceptable if other sports are not included. Therefore, this bill should surely not, I think, constitute a government priority.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote some comments I read recently, in particular one by Jean Barette, an experienced Montreal columnist. I think that he is right to ask himself several questions, and he would have desired to put some questions to the minister if the latter had been able to answer a recent invitation to come to Montreal. His absence was undoubtedly warranted.
This bill which is now before the House requires a minimum of Canadian players and sets the number of import players. Mr. Barette says, and I quote:
For example, The United States Congress could require that U.S. hockey clubs have a 60 per cent American roster. This would have tragic consequences for many Canadians who earn a very good living in the United States and who pay their taxes in our country, which provide some nice dollars to Mr. Lalonde and several politicians like him.

First of all, the following question could have been put to Mr. Lalonde:-
-and we wish we could have asked it.
... "Will you meet the deficit of the Montreal Olympic stadium following the 1976 Olympic Games?
We are quite aware of the fact that for the Olympic Games Montreal will have a most adequate stadium. I am happy to see that Toronto has a chance of getting a professional team and I wish them good luck. We know that cities like Montreal and Vancouver can have their professional football teams but this bill will not allow it. I know that the Island of Montreal at present does not have any Conservative member and I wonder if a plot is not being weaved against Montreal and the interests of the football fans of this city on account of the members remaining silent in this House. I believe it is important that the hon. members should express their views on this subject, because I have met Montreal members and they are against the passing of this bill. Of course the party line will be respected and they will vote for the bill. I know that three Montreal members are absolutely against it. I will not name them because I am discreet. Other members, also from Quebec, are not in favour of the bill. But we know the influence of the minister in the cabinet. I will not blame him for it but I know that as usual the orders given will be followed and they will deprive Montreal of any chance of having a professional football team.
People are concerned about professional teams. The Montreal Expos seem to be a good business proposition. We have witnessed a new motivation on the part of the young in baseball immediately after the coming of the Expos. Thousands of young Canadians are interested in baseball because Montrealers are proud of their professional team. The City of Montreal has become famous because of them. Every hon. member enjoys watching the Expos and seeing them win most of the time.
I am of the opinion that a professional football team would stir up the same motivation and I doubt that it would cause the death of the Canadian Football League. This is a false assumption. We know full well that businessmen would not invest huge amounts of money in cities where the endeavour would not be profitable. Cities should have been chosen which are able to encourage professional clubs. But no. The easy way out is preferred, by removing the possibility of competition, of rivalry between teams and sportsmen.
It is therefore not a waste of the time of the House to oppose such a bill that is moved by a minister who is certainly ill-advised. I have suffered too much from this type of thing when I was young. I too dreamed of going into professional sport, at the early age of 20. But there were only six professional hockey teams: many were called but few chosen. Today, the teams having multiplied, young talented Canadians have had the opportunity of bettering themselves and representing Canada admirably well throughout the world.
Therefore, these opportunities must be real for those young Canadians who play football, and this bill will eliminate those opportunities. The unwavering answer will be that the Canadian Football League will be able to
April 19, 1974

expand in Canada. We know full well that youth want perfection and that a player with a legitimate ambition cannot be satisfied with playing in a minor league. This league can be the best in the country but there can be a better one, and the sportsman who has plenty of guts will not be satisfied with playing in the first one. Personally, I am happy as a Canadian to see those superstars play all over Canada and abroad.
I believe that passage of the bill we are discussing now would be unnacceptable.
I would like to add a few words to Mr. Barrette's remarks which I just mentioned.
As for the second question that Mr. Barrette would have liked to ask the minister, I will ask it in his place:
Will you make up the deficit of the Olympic stadium?
I mean the stadium which would or could be used by such a team.
Will you take action against all sports such as golf, which comes under the control of the Royal Canadian Golf Association, which bows before the American PGA for the Canadian Open and submits to ridiculous restrictions on the number of Canadian golfers entitled to take part in the National Open of their own country? . .. we doubt that he could reply in the affirmative since the federal government, like Pontius Pilate, has washed its hands of everything that concerns the 1976 Olympic games organization. However, if Mr. Lalonde's bill eventually becomes law, it will deprive Montreal of a good source of revenue since the National Football League or the World Football League already have their eyes on the spacious stadium which will be completed in time for the Olympic games. It would have been very profitable to have an American football franchise. And this would not have prevented Mr. Berger from making his Alouettes play in the same stadium, even if the caliber of the Canadian league is clearly inferior. Some fans prefer the Canadian game to the American, whatever the quality of the players.
If the federal government does not help Montreal in the form of subsidies, the financial charge will naturally fall on the shoulders of Montrealers many of whom are supporters of our dear national "boy scout".
As for the second question, Mr. Lalonde could not have replied because, first of all, he must not even be aware of the existence of golf, even less of that of the Royal Canadian Golf Association, whose pundits have just announced that the Canadian Open will always be held in Toronto the Pure starting in 1980.
If Mr. Lalonde deigns to look into this problem of the takeover of the organization of our national Omnium by the American PGA, he will have to legislate in order to put an end to this infamous practice.
Mr. Speaker, this proves that when we discuss a bill relating only to football, arguing that it will allow thousands of Canadians to develop, we are making a mistake. At no time can the government introduce measures on recreation, physical fitness, the assessment of basic tools that we now have, or on the appropriations for our recreational organizations, in order to enable young people to develop properly.
I remember that not long ago, the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier) had called for an assessment of our recreational organizations. He talked about the addition of some buildings, if necessary, but unfortunately he will probably do the same as other members; he will not say a word because our time must be saved for other great current problems.
However, I think it is the right time to ask the responsible minister not to introduce such a bill, but rather to apply himself more, to increase appropriations and grant them to the department responsible for physical fitness. I
Canadian Professional Football think that this affects all citizens, whatever their age, not only children but also older citizens. It is very important that we agree to establish such a policy. It will be argued that we spend millions of dollars on OFY and LIP programs, but nobody ever says that half of this money is wasted because of poor submissions and selections.
I think it would be more profitable to affect those millions of dollars to a department for physical fitness, but not under the terms of a bill such as this one, because we know very well that the government has no business telling competent people how to organize a football or hockey league.
There are knowledgeable people who can take care of that. Our responsibility, of course, is to provide the thousands of Canadians who practice this sport each and every opportunity to give a first-rate performance. It is not up to us to tell them what to do.
That is why this is a ridiculous bill. We would have hoped that the minister would allocate additional funds. We are accused of wasting the time of the House; if the minister is willing to withdraw the bill, we would be quite happy to proceed to the consideration of much more important problems. But let not the minister believe that I will support his bill which goes against the liberties of all sportsmen. I think the minister will have the opportunity to read many reports from knowledgeable sport commentators which will enable him to think twice about it and to withdraw his bill. Even if it takes two weeks or two months, I will do everything to prevent the passage of this bill, which is not the right answer to the young people who are expecting new forms of assistance as well as justified and justifiable measures. We hear about encouraging young people to engage in recreative activities; that is surely not a way of accomplishing that, Mr. Speaker.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member allow me to ask a very serious question?
Yes, I would like him to ask his question. I have doubts about its seriousness, Mr. Speaker, but I allow him to ask it.

You will see later on.
Mr. Speaker, a while ago the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) seemed to ridicule the relationship between Canadian football-
Question, question!

That question is similar to that of the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield)!
-and national unity. Could he tell me if he agrees with the statement from the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) who said in 1961, and I will repeat it in Shakespeare's language, which is the language of the former Prime Minister of Canada-
The annual Grey Cup game is a great national event for all Canadians. It stimulates an interest in sports, for it has become symbolic of athletic competition. It brings east and west together and contributes to the unity of the nation.
Does he agree with that?

The answer is quite clear, Mr. Speaker. The former Prime Minister of Canada was quite right but why ask such a question? Why does this bill mention only national unity about football, while east-west competition has national overtones? In my opinion, a simple legislation

You have another question?

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary. Should we understand that he disagrees and, by the way, this would not be the first disagreement within the
Progressive Conservative Party-

speechtext: Order.
Mr. Speaker, it is too bad we could not have more speakers from the opposite side of the House.
Hear, hear!

As my colleagues have pointed out, it is too bad that some of those who believe very strongly that this legislation, Bill C-22, is a mockery of parliament are not allowed to speak. If the minister would like to call the debate to a close, all he has to do is ask for the floor, which I will gladly relinquish, and withdraw the legislation.
In the first place, we should not be here at all this week. It was planned that we would have a recess, and I think there was need for a recess. During such recess we could have met with our constituents, discussed the problems of the day and tried to find out what is going on in those parts of the country which do not revolve around Ottawa. Sometimes I think we are here too much. It is necessary to get away from Ottawa to find out what is going on. We had planned to do this. Many of us had not planned to go to Barbados or anywhere as exotic as that. Unfortunately, the government was afraid to meet a simple test of confidence, a test they have boastfully been able to accept until now-a test they now feel they may lose.
I want to make it clear for the record, although the few of us in the House this afternoon are aware of it, that the government sets the schedule and places the bills before the House. The government sets the priorities. The Easter recess could have been called. One opposition day prior to a budget would not have made a great difference if the government is as confident as it seems to be. We are now faced with the ridiculous situation whereby after the budget is presented there will be more opposition days than government legislation days, yet the government is worried because it does not have enough time now. We need legislation to deal with the problems of this country.
Let us take a minute to look at the legislation we have dealt with so far this session and see how important some of it is. Look at Bill C-2, the Fisheries Development Act. This provides funds for conversion of fishing vessels. It is very important for fishermen, but it does not do a thing for those with inadequate housing, those who every day fight inflationary food costs. Let us look at Bill C-5, the CN financing bill. It is a very necessary housekeeping type of bill. It was not passed in 1971, 1972 or 1973 and it

does not do a great deal toward providing the extra freight cars which are needed in the west. It certainly does not do anything to clear up the transportation mess the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) spoke of a few weeks ago.
Take Bill C-6, the national parks legislation. A lot of time was spent on this subject last session. But the bill does not do a thing to create land banks which would provide lots at lower cost for those wishing to own houses in Canada. Bill C-7 was designed to amend the Combines Investigation Act. A lot of time was spent on it. It should have been brought in last session because it was badly in need of revision, as are most of the bills brought forward by the government. It is restrictive and it does nothing to roll back major price increases which are likely to face us. Bill C-9, the Yukon and Northwest Territories legislation, increases the numbers of councillors in the north from 7 to 12 and from 14 to 15 respectively. It is probably very important for those who live in the north, but it does not do a thing to increase the number of officials employed by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs who inspect delivery equipment used in the supply of fuel oil to homes. Meters in my riding have not been tested for three years and are bound to be inaccurate by now.
Bill C-14, the one we discussed a week ago, raised the ceilings on loans to farmers, fishermen and small businessmen. I spoke at some length on that bill last week and I do not intend to go into the subject again. The legislation falls short in many respects. For example, it fails to allow a person to qualify if he works away from the farm and also operates a farm. The ceilings are still not high enough to be of much practical value to business. The banks are not obliged to lend money to people who need it. As usual, it is too little and too late.
Then there was Bill C-17, the VLA measure. This was extended at the eleventh hour. Finally, it was extended under pressure from my hon. friends and myself. It was necessary, but the bill could have been brought in last session and it should have been if the government had any sympathy whatsoever for the veterans of the country. Bill C-18 was a very important bill dealing with the export tax on oil. It was necessary following the decisions reached at the meeting of first ministers. But there was nothing new in the bill, no provision which would result in a supply of energy from new sources, nothing which would encourage the development of our nuclear potential, nothing for the northern part of Hastings county where uranium which could be used to provide an alternate source of energy for the country is lying untapped.
As for Bill C-19 to amend the Canada Pension Plan which we were discussing yesterday, it does improve things for people between age 65 and 69, and certain other improvements are to be brought about, and though it is necessary legislation which I expect we shall support, it needs review in committee. It does nothing to bring down the price of food for senior citizens. It does nothing to reduce the cost of other necessities of life for senior citizens.
So with these priorities we come to Bill C-22, the football bill, and we are asked by the minister to say absolutely nothing on it. Take a look at the bill. It is supposed to protect the Canadian Football League. I personally support the Canadian Football League, unlike some of my
April 19, 1974

colleagues and, indeed, unlike some of my constituents. I prefer Canadian football; I am not a follower of the National Football League. I deplore the fact that Canadian funds are going into the Olympics field in Montreal and that the field is only being built to NFL size.
One of my constituents telephoned me some time ago. He was worried about the CFL, quite naturally, because he is an ardent football fan. This bill does not protect the CFL. It merely attempts to keep out one team of the World Football League from the city of Toronto. The constituent who called me has suddenly turned about, because the government has absolutely no business getting into professional football, baseball, hockey, basketball or lacrosse. As has been said here many times, the government might do better if it took a greater interest in minor sports, the interest of many Canadians who spend hours of their time on Saturdays and weekends coaching young players with little or no help from the federal government.
In my home city of Belleville, in the heart of Hastings county, there is a group of citizens known as the Belleville Yardmen who, with other concerned people in the area, have raised over $1 million to build a major sports complex which will enable all manner of athletes to train to a level which would allow them to compete in the Olympics. If the federal government wants to get involved in the business of sport, this is the place where it might start.
The minister said in the course of his speech that this was an emotional issue, one which stirred up deep feelings. I have news for him. The majority of people in my riding could not care less whether the Northmen play in Toronto or not. I think that on a Friday afternoon they are much more concerned about the fact that it takes more money to buy less when they go to the grocery store. Perhaps the minister might suggest that since they cannot buy as many groceries, they get a smaller car to carry them in. That is the type of thinking we have been given recently.
The minister said there was incredible interest in this subject. The hon. member for York West (Mr. Fleming) said he had received only 40 letters on it and none on inflation. I do not know whether the hon. member for York West is particularly unpopular or whether his constituents know that he will do nothing to deal with the inflationary situation. As far as I am concerned, only six people have talked to me about this football question; five of them were opposed to it and the other one changed his mind. But I have had all kinds of letters, telephone calls and personal representations on the subject of inflation because people are genuinely concerned about it.
The minister went on to say that this football issue "epitomizes the central dilemmas of our 100 years as a nation". Then he added that it was "symbolic of our history". I shall not be as polite, perhaps, as some of my hon. friends. I have been trying to think of a term which would be parliamentary and which I could use. The only word I can come up with is "balderdash". I can think, of course, of many that are stronger, but I cannot use them within the confines of this august chamber.
I find it extraordinary that we should be asked to approve legislation which proposes, among other things, a two-year jail sentence, plus a fine, for those who set up an enterprise employing persons other than Canadians in
Canadian Professional Football order to provide employment or pleasure. I note, sadly, in this connection that a man may still kill two young people-as recently happened-and incur no greater penalty than a fine of $125. But this is typical of the government and of the minister's department.
One short aside, if I may. About a year and a half ago a meeting was held in the west block, I think it was. It was referred to as Sport Canada. The meeting was attended by some hockey stars, and photographers were present. I thought my son might get a chuckle out of seeing his dad with Jean Beliveau and Johnny Ferguson. Certainly he would be far more impressed in those circumstances than he would by seeing me with the Minister of National Health and Welfare, Mr. Lalonde. The photographers took some pictures, and when the meeting was over I asked whether I could have a copy of some of them. They sent me the proofs and I said, "Yes, that's the one I should like to have." That was a year and a half ago and I still do not have the picture. I think this is typical of the hon. gentleman's department-overkill in one area and complete loss in another.
An election is coming. The Minister of National Health and Welfare felt that this was the way to placate the west. I suggest he is not at all interested in the Canadian Football League or in any other sport for that matter. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been wrong before, he will be wrong again and he is wrong now. He is wrong to believe that Canadians will be fooled by this type of nonsense.
In Canada today we have strikes, transportation problems and inflation. What an opportunity for fine leadership. What a time for a leader to take firm hold and deal with these problems. Good leadership thrives on adversity. We are floundering. There is no way that I, for one, and my colleagues with me, will submit to the threats of this minister. He accuses us of holding up legislation by dealing with this bill at length. As I said, it is the government that sets up the schedule, so let it withdraw the bill. The CNR bill was discussed for three years. Let the government bring in new legislation to deal with problems in Canada.
I am not fond of sitting in an almost empty House on a Friday afternoon when I could be on the way to my riding. I do not notice the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Poulin) making any contribution, but if he wants to speak I will give him the floor. As I say, Mr. Speaker, I could be on the way to my riding where I would at least be providing some kind of useful service to my constituents. But I resent strongly the threat of the minister, and I will sit here as long as necessary until some good legislation comes forward from the government or they finally have the good grace to ask for the judgment of the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, there is not very much time left, so I shall not go into many of the things that I wanted to say. It is interesting to sit here and watch hon. members, especially the minister, across the way with their long faces and none of them speaking. This is because they realize the stupidity of the bill. They realize they have lost the confidence of

April 19, 1974
Canadian Professional Football
the people of the country, not only on other matters but on this bill as well. The people of this country do not support the intention of the government to keep the Toronto Northmen out of Canada, and certainly the people of British Columbia do not support this bill.
After what I have said, Mr. Speaker, it is pretty obvious that I will be voting against the bill, but I also want to inform the minister that in committee I intend to move approximately 50 amendments to his bill. A lot of them will be ridiculous amendments, but they will be moved in order to delay the bill. Then when we come back to the House for third reading, I will propose the same amendments and the hon. member sitting next to me will second them. I shall speak for the full allotted time on every one because I think we have to show the people of this country the stupidity of what this government is doing. If hon. members opposite ask me why don't I vote, I say I am not prepared to vote because the minister has twisted the arms of all his members across the way, insisting that they vote along with him and not in the way their conscience dictates.
The minister talks about the number of Canadians and the number of Americans who should be on a team. What does he know about it, Mr. Speaker? I think I know a little about it because I played football in my younger days. I just cannot understand why he says there should be 15 Americans and 70 Canadians. That is none of the government's business. If he is going to make that provision, perhaps we should amend the bill to provide that there must be six women playing for every team because we have to be fair to the women of this country.
Hear, hear!
Perhaps we should amend the bill to provide that there be two or three men over 45 on every team so as to be fair to the older people of this country.
Hear, hear!

Football players in Canada cannot collect unemployment insurance. Perhaps we should amend the bill to provide that they can collect unemployment insurance. Perhaps they should also be allowed workmen's compensation. We could amend this bill in many ways.
I think the best thing we could do with the bill is to have the minister put it back on the shelf and wait until after the election. Then we will find out what will happen from the people of this country. The minister is going to ban an American team from playing in Canada. Is he going to ban the team of Simon Fraser University, one of the best college teams in Canada, from playing football in the United States? The people of British Columbia would like to know, because they are quite happy when American teams come into British Columbia to play college games. They play American rules, and we happen to like them as well.
We also happen to like our hockey in British Columbia. We have two professional teams, one in the world league and one in the national league. We get the largest crowds of any team in the World Hockey League. We get large crowds to watch the Vancouver Blazers play. The Canucks are sold out for every game-15,540 people and 2,000 stan-

dees. It has been that way since the team came there. We support two teams. The funny thing about it is that the National Hockey League team is owned by Americans. Is the minister complaining about that? No, he does not think that is so bad. The World Hockey League team is owned by a Canadian, as I think are most or all of the World Hockey League teams in Canada. The teams in Edmonton, Winnipeg, Toronto and Vancouver are owned by Canadians. What has the government done for the World Hockey League? Nothing at all.
In the National Hockey League Stanley Cup finals there are four American teams. They will be competing tomorrow night, next week, and so on. The CBC will be covering every game. The Toronto Toros are playing in the World Hockey League. They have made the semi-finals of the championships, yet the CBC will not televise one of their games across Canada. People in Winnipeg, Edmonton and Vancouver deserve to see a Canadian team in the World Hockey League.
The hon. member for York West is mumbling and grumbling across the way. I can understand how sad he is at having to support the government's bill. Living in the area he does, he knows damned well what he will get when he goes back to his riding.
